rows.grounds: part or aspect of existence; bhāva-aṃśa
whose essence is one's own nature; svarūpa-ātman

items.question: Who manifests the clear appearance of dependence even in the self-created realm of being?
premises: The portion of being is self-created and essentially one's own nature.
Even there a clear appearance of dependence arises.
That appearance is manifested by the Lord alone.
items.inference: Dependence in the self-created realm is not imposed from outside but is manifested by the Lord himself.
items.plain_english: Therefore, even in the self-created portion of being, which is essentially one's own nature, this clear appearance of dependence is manifested by the Lord alone.

items.question: What is the defining mark of autonomy and dependence in the supreme Lord?
premises: The self-dependent supreme Lord fashions dependence.
Autonomy and dependence are both considered here.
No other defining mark is stated for them.
items.inference: The sole defining mark of dependence and autonomy is that the autonomous Lord freely fashions dependence.
items.plain_english: The self-dependent supreme Lord fashions dependence; no other defining mark is stated for autonomy and dependence than this.

rows.grounds: one whose light is circumscribed; paricchinna-prakāśa

items.question: What follows if the limiter itself is clearly limited?
premises: What has limited light is inert.
A limiter is posited here as standing over the limited.
If that limiter is itself clearly limited, it shares the same condition.
items.inference: Treating the limiter as itself limited threatens to collapse the distinction between limiter and limited.
items.plain_english: For what has limited light is inert; therefore, if the limiter posited here is itself clearly something to be limited, a problem arises.

items.question: Why does light fail to shine in grasping the form of a limited object?
premises: If the limiter is limited, light does not shine in grasping its form.
An external portion of being does not shine by itself.
Self-manifestation is absent in the merely external object.
items.inference: Because the external object lacks self-luminosity, its apprehension cannot be grounded in it alone.
items.plain_english: Then, in grasping its form, light does not shine; for an external portion of being does not shine by itself.

rows.grounds: having the illumination of objects as its essence; artha-prakāśa-ātman
ca-anābhāta; not appearing; sandhi within token

items.question: Can knowledge whose nature is object-illumination shine by its own nature if it is unmanifest?
premises: Knowledge is taken as having the illumination of objects as its nature.
If that knowledge is unmanifest, it does not appear.
Even its inherent self does not shine by its own nature.
items.inference: Knowledge cannot ground manifestation if it is itself unmanifest and not self-luminous.
uncertainties: The truncated form samavāyy is read as samavāyin/samavāyī in sandhi; analysis follows that reading.
items.plain_english: Knowledge is of the nature of illuminating objects, yet if it is unmanifest, even its inherent self does not shine by its own nature.

rows.grounds: the instrument belonging to that; tadīya-karaṇa

items.question: Can sense instruments or external aids manifest anything without consciousness?
premises: The instrument such as the eye does not shine by itself.
External aids such as light do not manifest objects on their own.
Without consciousness there is no manifestation at all.
items.inference: Neither sense organs nor external conditions can account for manifestation apart from consciousness.
items.plain_english: Its instrument, such as the eye, does not shine by itself; and without consciousness there is no manifestation at all, even with light and other aids.

items.question: What objection arises if an object's luminosity is treated as its own power or property?
premises: An opponent may claim that when knowledge arises, the object becomes manifest.
The opponent may treat that manifestness as the object's own power or property.
If every object had such a property, universal omniscience would follow.
items.inference: Making luminosity an intrinsic property of objects leads to the absurd consequence of omniscience throughout the world.
items.plain_english: But if, when knowledge arises, that luminosity of the object is its own power or property, then omniscience would follow throughout the whole universe.

rows.grounds: designated by the term luminosity; prakāśatva-abhiśabdita
among known, knower, and knowing; meya-mātṛ-māna

items.question: Can luminosity be coherently located as some separate entity among object, subject, and cognition?
premises: One might posit luminosity as some other entity.
The candidates for locating it are the known, the knower, and the act of knowing.
It does not fit coherently in any of these.
items.inference: Luminosity cannot be explained as a separate entity situated within the object-subject-cognition triad.
items.plain_english: Or if that so-called luminosity is taken as something else, it does not fit coherently anywhere among the known, the knower, and the means of knowing.

items.question: What dilemma follows if beings are intrinsically unmanifest yet somehow become illuminated?
premises: If luminosity is not grounded, the whole universe would always remain unmanifest.
If an intrinsically unmanifest being were to become illuminated, that is a further problem.
The opponent faces a dilemma between permanent non-manifestation and altered nature.
items.inference: Treating beings as intrinsically unmanifest makes either universal non-manifestation or loss of nature unavoidable.
items.plain_english: Therefore this whole universe would always remain unmanifest; and if an unmanifest being were to become illuminated, another difficulty follows.

rows.grounds: remaining in its essential form; svarūpa-stha

items.question: Does the arising of knowledge preserve or destroy the nature of a being that remains in its own form?
premises: If illumination changes an unmanifest being, its own nature would be lost.
If knowledge arises while the being remains in its own nature, that is called manifestation.
The opponent must explain manifestation without altering the being's nature.
items.inference: Manifestation cannot be explained as a change in the object's nature while it remains what it is.
items.plain_english: By that much its own nature would be lost; and if the arising of knowledge is the manifestation of a being while it remains in its own nature, that must be explained.

rows.grounds: in an entity remaining in its essence; svarūpa-stha-bhāva
grounded in the delimiting principle; paricchedaka-niṣṭhita

items.question: Why would manifestation not occur universally if beings remain undifferentiated in their own nature?
premises: If a being remains undifferentiated in its own nature, no selective manifestation is explained.
Manifestation of the whole universe would then be inexplicable or universal.
Therefore the light of the universe must be grounded in a limiter.
items.inference: The manifestation of the universe is grounded in the delimiting principle, not in undifferentiated objective being.
items.plain_english: If a being remains undifferentiated in its own nature, why would that manifestation not belong to the whole universe? Therefore the light of the universe rests in the limiter.

items.question: What follows if the limiter differentiated by freely manifested forms is itself limited?
premises: The limiter is differentiated by varied forms arising from its own free manifestation.
One might still suppose that this limiter is itself limited.
That supposition would generate a further regress.
items.inference: If the freely manifesting limiter is treated as limited, the account of limitation becomes unstable.
items.plain_english: If the limiter, differentiated by varied forms arising from the manifestation of its own freedom, were itself something to be limited, then a consequence follows.

items.question: Why must the ultimate limiter be called unlimited?
premises: If the limiter were itself limited, a root-destroying infinite regress would follow.
An infinite regress cannot ground manifestation.
Therefore the limiter must be unlimited.
items.inference: To avoid infinite regress, the ultimate delimiting principle must itself be unlimited.
items.plain_english: Then this root-destroying infinite regress would occur; therefore that limiter is said to be unlimited.

rows.grounds: not to be conceptually fabricated; a-kalpya
the condition of having knowable properties; vedya-dharma-tva

items.question: Why is the unlimited limiter not within the domain of time according to the scriptures?
premises: The unlimited limiter is not conceptually constructible as a limited object.
Therefore it is not within the domain of time.
The knowable-property status belongs to time, not to that limiter.
items.inference: Time governs knowable, delimited properties, so the unlimited limiter cannot fall under time's domain.
items.plain_english: Therefore it is not constructible and, as the scriptures say, not within the domain of time; for that reason the condition of being a knowable object is explained as belonging to time.

items.question: What follows if time is supposed to delimit the knowing subject?
premises: Suppose time delimits the subject.
Time's own stability would then depend on that subject.
Time would require the subject's functioning to operate.
items.inference: Time cannot be the ultimate delimiter of the subject, because its operation presupposes the subject.
items.plain_english: If time were to delimit the subject, then the stability of time would certainly depend on the subject and would require the subject's functioning.

items.question: How can infinite regress be avoided if another subject is posited to ground time?
premises: Positing another subject to ground time would not be possible without infinite regress.
Infinite regress must be removed to make the account coherent.
Therefore the subject must be accepted as free from temporal division.
items.inference: To avoid regress, the knowing subject must ultimately be free from time's delimitation.
items.plain_english: And no other subject could be posited, because of infinite regress; to remove that regress, this subject must be accepted as free from the divisions of time.

rows.grounds: in being both knower and known; mātṛ-meya-tva

items.question: How can one entity be both subject and object if time is attached to a limited subject?
premises: A limited subject may be taken as dependent on time.
If time makes that same entity both subject and known, a dual role is assigned.
In a strict difference-based view, one entity cannot coherently hold both roles.
items.inference: The opponent's difference-based framework cannot explain one entity functioning as both subject and object under time.
items.plain_english: But if the limited subject is indeed dependent on that time, then how, in your view, can one and the same entity be both subject and object?

rows.grounds: in the view based on difference; bheda-vāda
of those who hold non-difference; abheda-vādin

items.question: Why does the subject-object objection not refute the non-difference position?
premises: The objection presupposes a fixed commitment to difference.
That commitment belongs to the difference-doctrine.
For those who hold non-difference, the same objection does not apply.
items.inference: The objection is effective only within a difference framework and does not refute the non-difference view.
items.plain_english: For in the doctrine of difference your view is fixed in that way; but for us, who uphold non-difference, let there be no such refutation at all.

rows.grounds: by entangling nets of time and limiting factors; kāla-kalā-jāla-jambāla

items.question: Why is the supreme Lord not bound by time and limiting factors in the non-difference view?
premises: For this view, the universe consists of the subject.
Likewise the subject consists of the universe.
The supreme Lord is not entangled by the nets and mire of time and limitation.
items.inference: Because subject and universe are mutually contained in the supreme Lord, time and limitation do not bind him.
items.plain_english: For those for whom the universe consists of the subject and the subject likewise consists of the universe, the supreme Lord is not entangled in the mire of the nets of time and limiting factors.

rows.grounds: the luminosity of the power of consciousness; citi-śakti-prakāśa

items.question: How can the light of consciousness appear concealed and later manifest?
premises: The light of the power of consciousness takes on an appearance of tarnish.
Because of that, it appears concealed at one stage.
Afterward it appears in manifest form.
items.inference: Concealment and manifestation are modes of appearance of the same consciousness-power, not changes in its essence.
items.plain_english: For the light of the power of consciousness takes on a kind of tarnish; therefore it appears concealed at that time and later appears in manifest form.

rows.grounds: consisting in reflective awareness of one's own nature; svarūpa-āmarśana-ātmikā

items.question: What is the unfolding that designates concealment and manifestation in consciousness?
premises: The described concealment and manifestation are an unfolding of that same consciousness.
This unfolding designates such a condition.
It is a certain creative construal whose nature is reflective awareness of one's own form.
items.inference: The apparent change is the Lord's own reflective creative activity, not an external alteration.
items.plain_english: Thus this unfolding, which designates that condition, belongs to that same reality alone; it is a certain creative construal of its own, whose nature is reflective awareness of its own form.

rows.grounds: the self takes itself to be; ātmā-abhimanyate

items.question: How does the self come to regard itself in varied ways while remaining fit for union with Śiva?
premises: In that reflective construal the self regards itself as fit for union with Śiva.
Through association with variety the self regards itself in particular ways.
These self-regardings are modes of the same self's construal.
items.inference: The self's varied self-understandings arise through its own reflective construal in connection with variety.
items.plain_english: In that construal the self regards itself as fit for union with Śiva; for through connection with variety it comes to regard itself in that way.

rows.grounds: of the fall/descent of grace-power; śakti-pāta

items.question: Why is the descent of power said to have a ninefold arrangement without implying partiality in the Lord?
premises: The descent of power is taught here as ninefold.
If this variety were due to preference, the Lord would have attachment or aversion.
The Lord has no attachment or aversion anywhere.
items.inference: The ninefold arrangement of śaktipāta reflects the structure of reception, not partiality in the Lord.
items.plain_english: Therefore the descent of power is taught here as ninefold; otherwise the Lord would have attachment or aversion somewhere, which he does not.

items.question: What would follow if the all-pervading Lord sent down his power in a fixed and motivated way?
premises: If the Lord caused his own power to descend in a fixed manner somewhere, that would imply a determining cause.
The Lord is not subject to attachment, aversion, or external motive.
Therefore the descent of power is without external cause.
items.inference: The great Lord's descent of power is causeless with respect to external motives, though it appears in ordered forms.
items.plain_english: For if this all-pervading Lord were to send down his own power in a fixed way anywhere, that would imply a motive; thus this descent of power of the great Lord is without external cause.
